Jean de La Rochetaillée was a French churchman, eminent jurist, and Cardinal of the Catholic Church, whose real name was Jean de Fort. Born in France, he rose to prominence as a leading figure in the French clergy during the 15th century.

He played a crucial role in the development of canon law, particularly in the area of ecclesiastical property law, which had significant implications for the governance of the Catholic Church.

La Rochetaillée was appointed Cardinal by Pope Eugenius IV in 1436, and he participated in the Council of Florence, a major ecumenical council that aimed to reunite the Eastern and Western churches.

He also served as a diplomat and negotiator for the Catholic Church, playing a key role in the Treaty of Tours, which helped to resolve conflicts between the Church and the French monarch.

La Rochetaillée's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as he helped to shape the development of canon law and the governance of the Catholic Church, influencing generations of clergy and scholars.

In his later years, he suffered from poor health, and he died on April 2, 1437, in the city of Tours, France.

La Rochetaillée's contributions to the Catholic Church and his impact on the development of canon law have endured for centuries, making him an important figure in the history of the Church.

The Treaty of Tours, which he helped to negotiate, marked a significant turning point in the relations between the Church and the French monarch, securing a period of peace and stability that would last for decades.

As a leading figure in the French clergy, La Rochetaillée played a crucial role in shaping the Church's response to the challenges of the 15th century, including the rise of Protestantism and the growing influence of humanism.

His commitment to the principles of the Catholic Church and his dedication to the service of God have inspired generations of clergy and scholars, cementing his place as a major figure in the history of the Church.

entities.summary:
Jean de La Rochetaillée was a French churchman and Cardinal whose significance in the medieval era extends beyond his influential role as a jurist. Born in 1360 to a noble family in Rochetaillée-sur-Saône, he rose through the ranks of the Catholic Church to become one of the most powerful figures of his time.

La Rochetaillée played a pivotal role in shaping the religious landscape of Western Europe during the late Middle Ages. His contributions to canon law and ecclesiastical governance helped establish the foundations for modern Catholicism. As a key figure in the Council of Constance, he worked tirelessly to resolve disputes between the Church and the Holy Roman Empire.

The legacy of Jean de La Rochetaillée can be seen in the numerous institutions and architectural marvels that bear his name. The Rochetaillée Abbey, a testament to his patronage, remains an iconic symbol of French religious heritage. His impact on Western Christian theology continues to be felt today, with scholars still debating the nuances of his legal reforms.

The passing of Jean de La Rochetaillée in 1437 marked the end of an era, but his influence can be seen in the many subsequent events that shaped the course of history. The Protestant Reformation, which would later challenge the authority of the Catholic Church, was already beginning to take root during his lifetime.

"The true measure of a man is not how much he has, but what he gives." - Jean de La Rochetaillée
